questions.stem: Why is water classified as a renewable resource?
options: The water cycle continually replenishes it
It never runs out anywhere
It can be manufactured
It is found underground
questions.explanation: Renewability comes from the cycle. Water can still be locally scarce if used faster than it is replenished.

questions.stem: What drives the water cycle?
options: The Moon's gravity
Wind alone
Energy from the Sun
Energy from the Earth's core
questions.explanation: Solar energy powers evaporation, which drives the whole cycle.
questions.teaching:
The water cycle moves water endlessly between oceans, air, land and living things, and it needs an energy source to keep running.

That energy drives evaporation, lifting water from oceans and lakes into the air as vapour — which is the step that makes everything else possible. Gravity then does the returning work, pulling rain down and rivers seawards. So the cycle is powered from above and returned from below. Without the input, evaporation would stop and the whole cycle would halt.

questions.stem: What is evaporation in the water cycle?
options: Liquid water changing into water vapour
Water vapour changing into liquid
Water falling as rain
Water soaking into soil
questions.explanation: Condensation is the reverse process and precipitation is water falling.

questions.stem: What is precipitation?
options: Water falling from clouds as rain, hail or snow
Water evaporating from oceans
Water soaking into the ground
Water flowing in rivers
questions.explanation: Precipitation is the falling stage of the cycle.

questions.stem: What does 'liveability' mean in geography?
options: How old a place is
How suitable a place is for people to live in
How many people live in a place
The size of a place
questions.explanation: Liveability is assessed on measures like access to services, environmental quality and safety.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental measure of liveability?
options: The size of the population
Air and water quality
The number of shops
The local election result
questions.explanation: Environmental quality is one of the named measures, alongside economic and social factors.

questions.stem: What is water scarcity?
options: A shortage of water relative to demand in a place
Water that is too deep to reach
Water that has evaporated
Rain falling at the wrong time of year
questions.explanation: Scarcity is about the relationship between supply and demand, not just total rainfall.

questions.stem: What is a landform?
options: A natural feature of the Earth's surface
A building constructed by people
A type of soil
A weather pattern
questions.explanation: Mountains, valleys, cliffs and dunes are landforms.
questions.teaching:
Geography distinguishes between features made by nature and features made by people.

Natural features of the Earth's surface — mountains, valleys, dunes, plateaus, river deltas, cliffs — form one category, shaped by processes like erosion, deposition, tectonic movement and weathering over long periods. Built features such as roads, dams and cities form another. The test is whether people made it, and the answer decides which set of processes explains how it got there.

questions.stem: What is urbanisation?
options: The decline of city populations
The growth in the proportion of people living in cities
The building of new farms
The movement of people to the countryside
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is about the shift of population towards urban areas.

questions.stem: What is migration?
options: A daily journey to work
A holiday to another country
Movement of goods between countries
The movement of people from one place to another to live
questions.explanation: Migration involves changing where you live, and can be internal or international.

questions.stem: What is internal migration?
options: Movement of people within the same country
Movement between countries
Movement of goods
Seasonal movement of animals
questions.explanation: Moving from a regional town to a capital city is internal migration.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an atmospheric hazard?
options: An earthquake
A landslide
A volcanic eruption
A cyclone
questions.explanation: Cyclones, storms and droughts are atmospheric or hydrometeorological. Earthquakes and volcanoes are geological.
questions.teaching:
Natural hazards are classified by their source, and the category names are built from the Greek words for those sources.

'Atmos' gives the air, so that category covers hazards produced by weather and climate — cyclones, storms, heatwaves, droughts, blizzards. 'Geo' gives the earth, covering earthquakes, volcanoes and landslides. 'Hydro' gives water, covering floods and tsunamis. 'Bio' gives life, covering disease. So identifying the category means asking which system generated the event.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a geomorphological hazard?
options: A thunderstorm
A landslide
A heatwave
A drought
questions.explanation: Geomorphological hazards involve landforms and earth processes.
questions.teaching:
Natural hazards are grouped by which part of the Earth system produces them, and the prefixes tell you which.

Hazards from the atmosphere include cyclones, storms, heatwaves and droughts. Hazards from water include floods and tsunamis. Hazards involving living things include plagues and disease outbreaks. And hazards produced by movement of the Earth's surface and materials — earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides — form their own group. Reading the prefix in each category name tells you which system it belongs to.

questions.stem: What is a drainage basin (catchment)?
options: The mouth of a river
An area with no rainfall
The area of land from which water drains into a river system
A storage tank for drinking water
questions.explanation: Everything that falls in the catchment eventually flows to the same river.

questions.stem: What does 'sustainability' mean when managing a resource?
options: Using as much as possible now
Never using the resource
Selling the resource overseas
Using it in a way that does not compromise its availability in future
questions.explanation: Sustainability balances present use against future availability.

questions.stem: What is erosion in a landscape?
options: The wearing away and transport of material by water, wind or ice
The building up of new land
The freezing of soil
The growth of vegetation
questions.explanation: Erosion removes and transports; deposition builds up.

questions.stem: What is deposition?
options: The melting of ice
The evaporation of water
The laying down of transported material
The wearing away of rock
questions.explanation: Beaches and river deltas are formed by deposition.

questions.stem: What is a spiritual or cultural value of a landscape?
options: Its height above sea level
The rainfall it receives
Its meaning and significance to people, including connection to Country
The money it generates
questions.explanation: The curriculum names spiritual, aesthetic and cultural value alongside economic value.

questions.stem: What is social connectedness in a community?
options: The number of roads in an area
The speed of the internet
The distance to the nearest city
The strength of relationships and sense of belonging between people
questions.explanation: It is one of the influences on how liveable people find a place.

questions.stem: Which type of map shows height and shape of land using contour lines?
options: A road map
A topographic map
A political map
A weather map
questions.explanation: Contour lines join points of equal elevation.

questions.stem: Why can a country with high total rainfall still experience water scarcity?
options: High rainfall always prevents scarcity
High rainfall regions export their water elsewhere
Scarcity depends only on population
Rainfall may be seasonal or unevenly distributed relative to where people live
questions.explanation: Northern Australia receives heavy seasonal rain while southern cities face restrictions — distribution and timing matter as much as total.

questions.stem: How does climate change affect Australia's water resources according to forecasts?
options: Rainfall becoming perfectly predictable
Changes in rainfall patterns and increased variability in many regions
Uniformly increased rainfall everywhere
A steady decline in rainfall across every region equally
questions.explanation: Projections indicate shifting patterns and greater variability, which complicates water planning.

questions.stem: Two suburbs have similar incomes but different liveability ratings. What might explain this?
options: One suburb must have miscounted its population
Liveability is set by the local council each year
Differences in access to services, environmental quality or social connectedness
Liveability depends only on income
questions.explanation: Liveability is multi-dimensional, which is exactly why the curriculum lists several measures.

questions.stem: Why do perceptions of liveability differ between people in the same place?
options: People value different things depending on their circumstances and stage of life
Liveability is an objective fact
Only experts can judge liveability
Everyone values the same things
questions.explanation: A family with children and a university student weigh access to schools and nightlife very differently.

questions.stem: How does the concept of interconnection help explain a river's condition?
options: Activities upstream affect water quality and flow downstream
Rivers are unaffected by human activity
Each part of a river is independent
Interconnection applies only to cities
questions.explanation: Catchments link places, which is why upstream land use matters to downstream communities.

questions.stem: What is a common environmental impact of rapid urbanisation?
options: Improved air quality in every case
A reduction in energy use
An increase in farmland
Loss of vegetation and increased pressure on water and waste systems
questions.explanation: Rapid growth often outpaces infrastructure, producing pollution and service shortfalls.

questions.stem: Why do people migrate from rural areas to cities in urbanising countries?
options: Because governments require it
For employment, education and services not available in rural areas
Because cities always have lower living costs
Because rural areas have no population
questions.explanation: These are pull factors. Push factors such as declining agricultural work also contribute.

questions.stem: How does Australia's urban pattern differ from that of many other countries?
options: Most Australians live in rural areas
Australia has no large cities
Its population is highly concentrated in a few coastal cities
Its population is spread evenly across the continent
questions.explanation: Australia is one of the most urbanised countries, with most people in a handful of coastal centres.

questions.stem: What geomorphological process forms a river valley?
options: Deposition of sediment by wind
Volcanic eruption
Sudden tectonic uplift only
Erosion by flowing water over long periods
questions.explanation: Running water erodes downwards and outwards, shaping the valley over time.

questions.stem: Why is vegetation removal along a riverbank a problem?
options: Vegetation blocks the river and raises flood levels
It improves water quality
It increases river depth permanently
Roots stabilise soil, so removal increases erosion and sediment in the water
questions.explanation: Riparian vegetation holds banks together and filters runoff.

questions.stem: Which response would best reduce the impact of a flood hazard on a town?
options: Land use planning that avoids building on the floodplain, plus warning systems
Ignoring the risk
Building more houses on the floodplain
Removing all vegetation from the catchment
questions.explanation: Reducing exposure is the most effective response, supported by preparedness measures.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a hazard and a disaster?
options: A hazard only occurs in cities
A hazard is the natural event; a disaster is the serious harm it causes to people
They mean the same thing
A disaster always precedes a hazard
questions.explanation: A cyclone over an empty ocean is a hazard but not a disaster. Vulnerability and exposure make the difference.

questions.stem: Why is fieldwork valuable in a geographical inquiry?
options: It provides primary data about a place that secondary sources may not capture
It is quicker than using existing data
It removes the need for maps
It guarantees a correct conclusion
questions.explanation: Direct observation and measurement generate primary data specific to the question being asked.

questions.stem: How can improving public transport affect both liveability and sustainability?
options: It improves access to services while reducing emissions and congestion
It improves access to services but raises overall emissions
It lowers emissions but reduces access for outer suburbs
It improves both, but only for households without cars
questions.explanation: Some interventions serve several goals at once, which is why they are attractive to planners.

questions.stem: A study concludes a suburb is 'unliveable' based only on traffic data. What is the weakness?
options: A single indicator cannot capture a multi-dimensional concept
Traffic data is never accurate
Liveability depends only on traffic
Traffic data is collected too infrequently to be current
questions.explanation: Drawing a broad conclusion from one narrow measure is a common flaw in geographical reasoning.

questions.stem: How does the concept of scale change conclusions about water availability?
options: Only local scale matters
A country may have plenty nationally while particular regions face severe shortage
Larger scales always give more reliable water figures
National figures are always most accurate
questions.explanation: Aggregating hides variation, which is why geographers analyse at more than one scale.

questions.stem: Why is it important to consider ethical values when drawing conclusions in a geographical inquiry?
options: Ethical concerns are handled separately by government
Data alone determines the right decision
Ethical questions have single correct answers
Decisions about land and resources affect people unequally, and those impacts must be weighed
questions.explanation: The curriculum names ethical values explicitly. Who benefits and who bears the cost is a geographical question, not just a technical one.

questions.stem: What is condensation in the water cycle?
options: Water flowing into rivers
Water vapour cooling to form liquid droplets
Liquid water becoming vapour
Water falling as rain
questions.explanation: Condensation forms clouds; precipitation is water falling from them.

questions.stem: What is infiltration?
options: Water flowing over the surface
Water evaporating from a lake
Water freezing into ice
Water soaking into the ground
questions.explanation: Infiltration recharges groundwater; runoff flows over the surface instead.

questions.stem: What is runoff?
options: Water stored in clouds
Water flowing over the land surface into rivers
Water soaking into soil
Water evaporating
questions.explanation: Hard surfaces increase runoff, which is why cities flood quickly.

questions.stem: What is groundwater?
options: Water stored underground in soil and rock
Water in rivers and lakes
Water vapour in the air
Water frozen in glaciers
questions.explanation: Aquifers store groundwater, and some recharge very slowly.

questions.stem: What is a natural hazard?
options: A human-made disaster only
A type of landform
A natural event with potential to harm people or property
Any weather event
questions.explanation: It becomes a disaster only when it affects people significantly.

questions.stem: What is a floodplain?
options: A dry inland area
A coastal cliff
Flat land beside a river that floods periodically
The source of a river
questions.explanation: Floodplains are fertile but risky to build on.
questions.teaching:
Rivers shape the land around them, and the features they create have specific names.

Where a river runs through a wide valley, it periodically overflows and spreads sediment across the flat land on either side. That repeated flooding is what builds the flat surface and makes the soil fertile — which is why these areas have been farmed and settled for thousands of years despite the obvious risk. The name describes both the landform and the hazard, and the two cannot be separated.

questions.stem: What is an aquifer?
options: An underground layer of rock that holds water
A surface reservoir
A river mouth
A type of cloud
questions.explanation: Aquifers supply bore water in many parts of Australia.
questions.teaching:
Not all fresh water sits on the surface; a great deal is underground, and there is a term for the rock that holds it.

Water soaks down through permeable rock and collects in the pore spaces and cracks, forming a layer that can be tapped by wells and bores. Australia's Great Artesian Basin is one of the largest in the world and supports pastoral industry across much of the inland. Because these layers refill very slowly, extracting faster than the recharge rate depletes them — which is a live issue in Australian water policy.

questions.stem: What is population density?
options: The birth rate
The number of houses
The number of people per unit of area
The total population
questions.explanation: Density relates population to space, which is why large populations can still be sparse.
questions.teaching:
Two population measures sound similar and answer different questions.

One is simply how many people live somewhere — a raw count. The other divides that count by the area they occupy, giving people per square kilometre, which describes how crowded a place is rather than how big its population is. Australia has a moderate population and one of the lowest figures for the second measure on Earth, because that population is spread across a continent — which is exactly why the two must be kept separate.

questions.stem: What is a push factor in migration?
options: The distance travelled
Something that drives people to leave a place
Something that attracts people to a place
The cost of moving
questions.explanation: Lack of work is a push factor; better opportunities elsewhere is a pull factor.

questions.stem: What is a pull factor in migration?
options: The speed of travel
Something that attracts people to a new place
Something that drives people away
A physical barrier
questions.explanation: Jobs, services and safety are common pull factors.

questions.stem: Why do hard surfaces in cities increase flood risk?
options: Cities receive more rain
Hard surfaces evaporate water faster
Water cannot infiltrate, so more runs off quickly into drains and rivers
Concrete absorbs more water
questions.explanation: Reduced infiltration concentrates the same rainfall into a faster, larger flow.

questions.stem: Why are floodplains often densely settled despite the risk?
options: Flat, fertile land near water is attractive for farming and transport
Residents accept the risk because insurance covers the loss
Floods are rare enough to be ignored in planning
Building codes make floodplain housing cheaper to construct
questions.explanation: The advantages are real, which is why the risk persists and must be managed.

questions.stem: What does a high population density in a city suggest about liveability pressures?
options: That the city is always more liveable
That the city has no services
That the population is falling
Greater demand on housing, transport and services
questions.explanation: Density brings both efficiency and pressure, which is why it is managed rather than simply avoided.

questions.stem: How does access to green space affect liveability?
options: It improves property prices without changing daily life
It improves liveability only for households without gardens
It improves environmental quality and opportunities for recreation and social contact
It affects recreation but not environmental quality
questions.explanation: Green space touches environmental, social and health dimensions at once.

questions.stem: Why might a city's outer suburbs score lower on liveability measures?
options: Longer travel times and fewer nearby services
They always have worse weather
They have more green space
They have higher incomes
questions.explanation: Accessibility to services is one of the named liveability measures.

questions.stem: What is one impact of internal migration to Australian capital cities?
options: Increased pressure on housing and infrastructure in those cities
Decreasing city populations
Regional areas gain population at the same rate
Falling housing demand
questions.explanation: Movement affects both origin and destination — regional decline as well as urban growth.

questions.stem: Why is water in a river described as interconnected with land use?
options: Rivers are affected by land use only near their banks
Land use changes water quality but not the quantity
Activities across the catchment affect the water's quantity and quality
River conditions depend mainly on the season
questions.explanation: Interconnection is one of the key geographical concepts in the curriculum.

questions.stem: How can a geomorphological hazard be reduced in its impact?
options: By removing vegetation
By mapping risk areas and restricting or engineering development there
By ignoring the hazard
By building more housing in the risk zone
questions.explanation: Reducing exposure is generally more effective than trying to control the hazard itself.

questions.stem: Why is fieldwork data described as primary data?
options: It is collected first-hand by the investigator
It is published by government
It comes from a textbook
It is always numerical
questions.explanation: Secondary data has been collected and published by someone else.

questions.stem: What does a choropleth map show?
options: Areas shaded to represent the value of a variable
The height of land using contours
Individual points of data
The route of a journey
questions.explanation: Shading intensity represents the variable, which makes spatial patterns visible.

questions.stem: Why can improving one aspect of liveability sometimes reduce another?
options: Improvements benefit long-term residents before newer ones
Trade-offs exist, such as denser housing improving access but reducing green space
Conflicts arise only where funding is limited
Liveability improves overall even when one measure falls
questions.explanation: Recognising trade-offs is central to evaluating planning strategies.

questions.stem: Why is climate change described as a challenge for water planning rather than simply less rain?
options: Changing variability and timing complicate storage and supply even where totals hold
Rainfall totals are the only factor
Climate change increases rain everywhere
Planning is unaffected
questions.explanation: Infrastructure is built for historical patterns, and increased variability undermines those assumptions.

questions.stem: A proposal would improve a city's liveability but increase emissions. How should it be evaluated?
options: By weighing the benefits against sustainability costs, including who bears each
Liveability always outweighs sustainability
Sustainability always outweighs liveability
It should be rejected automatically
questions.explanation: The curriculum asks students to weigh factors and consider impacts, not apply a fixed rule.

questions.stem: Why do geographers study a local landform as well as global processes?
options: Local landforms form by processes unique to each site
Only local scale matters
Global processes are studied only from satellite data
Local study makes general processes observable and testable at a manageable scale
questions.explanation: The curriculum specifies a study of a local landform for exactly this reason.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support a claim that a river's water quality has declined?
options: Repeated measurements over time compared against an upstream control site
A single water sample
The river looking muddy after rain
Local opinion alone
questions.explanation: Trend data plus a comparison point separates a real change from natural variation.

questions.stem: Why is urbanisation described as having environmental, economic and social impacts together?
options: Environmental impacts appear first, with social effects following decades later
Concentrating people changes land, livelihoods and communities simultaneously
Economic impacts are measured while environmental ones are only estimated
The impacts are grouped together because governments report them as one figure
questions.explanation: Geographical analysis deliberately considers these dimensions together rather than in isolation.

questions.stem: What is transpiration?
options: Rain falling from clouds
Water vapour released from plants into the air
Water soaking into soil
Water flowing in rivers
questions.explanation: Transpiration and evaporation together are called evapotranspiration.

questions.stem: What is a catchment divide?
options: A flood barrier
The high ground separating one drainage basin from another
The mouth of a river
A dam wall
questions.explanation: Rain falling either side of the divide flows to different river systems.

questions.stem: What is a delta?
options: A steep river valley
A dry riverbed
A coastal cliff
A landform of deposited sediment where a river meets the sea
questions.explanation: Deltas form where a river slows and drops its sediment load.

questions.stem: What is a scale on a map?
options: The relationship between map distance and real distance
The colour key
The direction indicator
The title
questions.explanation: Scale allows real distances to be calculated from a map.

questions.stem: What does a compass rose on a map show?
options: Distance
Population
Direction
Height
questions.explanation: It orients the reader to north and the other directions.
questions.teaching:
Maps have a standard set of elements, and each answers a different question about how to read the map.

The title says what it shows. The legend explains the symbols. The scale tells you how much the ground has been shrunk. The source says where the data came from. And one element orients the map, showing which way is north so that bearings and descriptions like 'the northern suburbs' can be used. Without it, a map cannot be lined up with the ground at all.

questions.stem: What is a natural resource?
options: A government service
Something from the environment that people use
A manufactured product
A type of map
questions.explanation: Water, minerals, forests and soil are natural resources.

questions.stem: What is sustainability in resource use?
options: Exporting resources
Meeting present needs without preventing future needs being met
Using resources as fast as possible
Never using resources
questions.explanation: The definition balances present and future.

questions.stem: What is a hazard risk?
options: The chance of a hazard causing harm to people or property
The size of the hazard
The cost of insurance
The date of the last event
questions.explanation: Risk combines likelihood with exposure and vulnerability.

questions.stem: What is a megacity?
options: A city with the most industry
A city with over 10 million people
Any capital city
A city with over 1 million people
questions.explanation: Megacities are concentrated in rapidly urbanising regions.

questions.stem: What is a place's accessibility?
options: How old it is
Its population density
How easily people can reach services and facilities from it
How large it is
questions.explanation: Accessibility is one of the named liveability measures.

questions.stem: Why does deforestation in a catchment increase flood risk downstream?
options: Fewer trees means less interception and infiltration, so more runoff arrives faster
Trees cause floods
Deforestation reduces rainfall
Trees release stored water, adding to the flood
questions.explanation: Vegetation slows and stores water; removing it concentrates the flow.

questions.stem: How does a dam change a river system?
options: It alters flow, traps sediment and affects species that depend on natural cycles
It has no downstream effect
It only stores water
It increases sediment downstream
questions.explanation: Dams provide water security but change the whole system below them.

questions.stem: Why is water sometimes described as a shared resource across borders?
options: Water rights are decided by international treaty
Each state manages the section of river within it
Only groundwater crosses political boundaries
River systems cross political boundaries, so use in one area affects others
questions.explanation: The Murray-Darling Basin crosses several states, which is why management is a shared arrangement.

questions.stem: What does high liveability usually require in terms of environmental quality?
options: Low rainfall
Clean air and water, low noise and access to green space
High population density only
Large industrial areas
questions.explanation: Environmental quality is one of several dimensions assessed.

questions.stem: Why can urban sprawl reduce sustainability?
options: It spreads demand so no single area is overloaded
It affects farmland but not energy or water use
It consumes land, increases car dependence and raises infrastructure costs per person
It reduces density, which lowers pollution overall
questions.explanation: Low-density expansion has systematic environmental and economic consequences.

questions.stem: How can a geomorphological process create a distinctive landform?
options: Each landform is shaped by a single process acting once
Repeated erosion or deposition shapes rock into characteristic forms over time
Landforms are shaped mainly by sudden hazard events
Processes act uniformly, so landforms differ only in size
questions.explanation: Wave action producing sea stacks is a clear example.

questions.stem: Why do geographers use both maps and fieldwork?
options: Fieldwork confirms what maps already show
Maps are used for planning and fieldwork for reporting
Maps show pattern at scale; fieldwork gives detailed local observation
Maps give the data and fieldwork supplies the photographs
questions.explanation: The two methods answer different kinds of question.

questions.stem: Why can a strategy that improves one place's liveability worsen another's?
options: Improvements take effect only after several years
Nearby places benefit automatically from the improvement
The cost falls on the place that gains the benefit
Resources, traffic or waste may simply be shifted elsewhere
questions.explanation: Considering interconnection across places is central to geographical evaluation.

questions.stem: Why is per-person water use a more useful measure than total use for comparing countries?
options: Total use is always better
Per-person figures remove the need for national data
Per-person figures show how much each household wastes
It accounts for population differences, allowing fair comparison
questions.explanation: A large country will use more in total regardless of efficiency.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support a claim that a place's liveability has improved?
options: A change in the population
Multiple indicators measured before and after, compared against a similar place
One resident's opinion
A single new facility opening
questions.explanation: Multi-indicator, before-and-after comparison with a control is the strongest design.

questions.stem: Why does climate change complicate hazard planning?
options: Climate change makes hazards easier to forecast
Historical frequency and intensity may no longer predict future events
Hazards shift location but keep the same frequency
Planning must now cover a longer time horizon only
questions.explanation: Infrastructure designed for past conditions may be undersized for future ones.

questions.stem: Which of these is a continuous resource, one that is available no matter how much people use it?
options: Coal mined from the ground
Timber from plantation forests
Fresh water stored in a dam
Energy from sunlight
questions.explanation: Solar energy, wind and tides are continuous: using them today does not reduce what arrives tomorrow. Timber and dam water are renewable, because they are replaced over time, but they can still run short if used faster than they are replaced. Coal is non-renewable because it takes millions of years to form.

questions.stem: About what share of all the water on Earth is salt water?
options: About 97%
About 70%
About 50%
About 85%
questions.explanation: Roughly 97% of Earth's water is in the oceans and other salt water, leaving only about 3% as fresh water, and most of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers. The figure of 70% is how much of Earth's surface is covered by ocean, which is a different measurement.

questions.stem: In geography, what is 'green water'?
options: Water held in rivers, lakes and dams
Used water from showers, sinks and laundries
Water coloured by algal blooms in rivers
Rain stored in the soil and used by plants
questions.explanation: Green water is the rain that soaks into the soil and is taken up by plants, so it supports crops and pastures without irrigation. Water in rivers, lakes, dams and aquifers is called blue water. Used water from showers and laundries is grey water, which can be recycled for gardens.

questions.stem: What is the Great Artesian Basin?
options: A vast store of groundwater in porous rock layers
A chain of inland salt lakes filled by occasional floods
A network of dams and weirs on the Murray River
A shallow inland sea left from the last ice age
questions.explanation: The Great Artesian Basin lies beneath about a fifth of Australia, mostly in Queensland, and holds groundwater in porous sandstone layers. Bores tap it to supply towns and stations across dry inland areas. Lake Eyre sits above part of the basin, but the basin itself is underground water, not a lake.

questions.stem: A country has large rivers, but most of its villages have no piped water because there is no money for pumps, pipes or treatment plants. What kind of water scarcity is this?
options: Virtual water scarcity
Economic water scarcity
Physical water scarcity
Water scarcity caused by drought
questions.explanation: Economic water scarcity happens when water exists but people cannot reach it because of a lack of money, infrastructure or good management. Physical scarcity is the tempting answer, but that means there is not enough water in the area to meet demand, as in much of North Africa. Here the rivers are full; the problem is getting the water to people.

questions.stem: What does the Snowy Mountains Scheme do with water from the upper Snowy River?
options: Diverts it west to the Murray and Murrumbidgee
Pipes it north to supply Sydney's drinking water
Stores it to protect Canberra from river flooding
Releases it east to refill coastal wetlands
questions.explanation: The scheme diverts water that would flow east to the sea through tunnels under the mountains into the Murray and Murrumbidgee rivers, generating hydro-electricity on the way and supplying irrigation farms inland. This is an inter-basin transfer: water is moved from one river basin to another. It does not supply Sydney's drinking water, which comes mainly from Warragamba Dam.

questions.stem: Perth gets a large share of its drinking water from desalination plants. Why does desalination suit a city like Perth?
options: It makes fresh water from the sea regardless of rainfall
It uses less electricity than pumping water from inland dams
It removes the need to treat any water before use
It refills the city's groundwater aquifers instantly
questions.explanation: Perth's rainfall has declined since the 1970s, so a supply that turns seawater into fresh water whatever the weather makes the city less dependent on rain. Desalination is not low-energy: pushing seawater through membranes needs a lot of electricity, which is one of its main drawbacks. The leftover salty brine must also be managed carefully.

questions.stem: What is the 'virtual water' in a kilogram of rice?
options: The water absorbed by the rice when it is cooked
The water traded between farmers as entitlements
The rain that evaporates before reaching the crop
The water used to grow and process that rice
questions.explanation: Virtual water is the water used to make a product, so exporting rice or beef also exports the water used to produce it. Water entitlements are traded too, but that is water trading, a separate idea. Thinking in virtual water helps explain why dry countries may import water-hungry foods rather than grow them.

questions.stem: In 2018 Cape Town in South Africa warned of a coming 'Day Zero'. What did 'Day Zero' mean?
options: The day most household taps would be turned off
The day the city's desalination plant would open
The first day of the city's annual wet season
The day water prices would be set back to zero
questions.explanation: After three dry years, Cape Town's dams fell so low that the city planned to switch off household taps and make residents collect a daily ration from collection points. Strict limits on water use, higher prices and some late rain meant Day Zero never arrived. It shows the social and economic impacts of water scarcity on a modern city.

questions.stem: The Brewarrina fish traps (Baiame's Ngunnhu) on the Barwon River in New South Wales are best described as:
options: A set of river locks built so paddle-steamers could carry wool
Stone traps built and cared for by Aboriginal people over a very long time
A stone weir built by colonists in the 1800s to store river water for irrigation
A modern fishway that lets native fish swim past a large dam wall
questions.explanation: The traps are a network of stone walls and ponds that Ngemba people and neighbouring nations built, maintained and shared, using the river's flows to catch fish. They are on the National Heritage List and show long-term Aboriginal management of water Country. They are not a colonial weir; colonial-era changes to the river later damaged parts of the traps.

questions.stem: Australia is the driest inhabited continent, and in a typical year only a small share of its rainfall ends up as river flow. What is the main reason?
options: Rivers in Australia are blocked by dams that hold back almost all of their flow
Heat and plants return most of the rain to the air before it reaches rivers
Most of the rain soaks straight down into the Great Artesian Basin
Most of Australia's rain falls over the ocean before reaching the coast
questions.explanation: High temperatures and sunshine mean much of the rain evaporates from soil and water surfaces, and plants transpire much of the rest, so little is left to run off into rivers. Some rain does recharge groundwater, but only a small fraction reaches the Great Artesian Basin. This high evaporation, together with very variable rainfall, is why Australia needs large water storages.

questions.stem: A city's dams fill well in La Niña years but fall to very low levels during El Niño droughts. Which strategy would most reduce the city's dependence on rainfall?
options: Building a larger dam on the same river
Buying more water entitlements from farmers upstream
Collecting more stormwater runoff from city streets
Building a desalination plant on the coast
questions.explanation: A desalination plant draws on the ocean, so its output does not depend on rain at all. A larger dam can store more water in wet years, but it still only fills when it rains in the catchment. Water bought from upstream and stormwater both come from the same rainfall, so they shrink during the same droughts.

questions.stem: Where do tropical cyclones form?
options: Over cold polar seas
Along high mountain ranges
Over warm tropical oceans
Over hot inland deserts
questions.explanation: Cyclones need ocean water warmer than about 26.5 °C to supply heat and moisture, which is why they form over tropical seas, mostly between November and April in Australia. They weaken quickly once they move over land because they lose that supply of warm, moist air. Deserts are hot but have no water to evaporate.

questions.stem: What is a storm surge?
options: A rise in sea level pushed ashore by a cyclone
A huge wave caused by an undersea earthquake
A sudden flood from heavy rain in the hills
A very high tide caused by the pull of the Moon alone
questions.explanation: A cyclone's strong winds and very low air pressure pile up sea water and push it onto the coast, which can flood low-lying towns. A wave caused by an undersea earthquake is a tsunami, a different hazard. Storm surges are most dangerous when they arrive at the same time as a high tide.

questions.stem: Which national agency issues Australia's weather, flood and cyclone warnings?
options: Geoscience Australia
The CSIRO
The Australian Bureau of Statistics
The Bureau of Meteorology
questions.explanation: The Bureau of Meteorology forecasts the weather and issues warnings for cyclones, floods, severe storms and fire weather, which emergency services use to plan evacuations. Geoscience Australia monitors earthquakes, and the CSIRO is a research organisation. Early warnings are one of the most effective ways to reduce deaths from atmospheric hazards.

questions.stem: Which conditions create the highest bushfire danger?
options: Cool, still days straight after heavy rain
Humid days with light sea breezes
Cold, frosty mornings in winter
Hot, dry, windy days with low humidity
questions.explanation: Heat and low humidity dry out grass, leaves and timber, and strong winds carry embers far ahead of a fire front, which is why fire danger ratings rise sharply on such days. Cool, still or humid weather slows the spread of fire. The 2019–20 Black Summer fires followed drought and record heat.

questions.stem: During an El Niño event, eastern Australia is more likely to experience:
options: An early, strong northern monsoon
Below-average rainfall and drought
Above-average rainfall and floods
More tropical cyclones crossing the coast
questions.explanation: In an El Niño, warmer water shifts east across the Pacific, so less moist air rises near Australia and rainfall usually drops, raising the risk of drought. Floods and more cyclones are linked to the opposite pattern, La Niña. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole can also reduce rain, and the worst droughts often come when both line up.

questions.stem: How does a flash flood differ from a riverine flood?
options: It rises within hours after very heavy rain on a small area
It builds slowly over several weeks as water moves down a big river
It is caused when a cyclone pushes sea water onto the coast
It happens only in dry desert creek beds far from towns
questions.explanation: Flash floods come from intense rain falling faster than the ground and drains can cope with, so water rises within minutes or hours, often in steep valleys or cities with hard surfaces. Riverine floods build slowly as water from a large catchment moves downstream, giving more time to warn people. Flash floods can happen in deserts, but also in cities and hills.

questions.stem: On the Australian scale, a Category 5 tropical cyclone is one with:
options: The slowest movement over land
The strongest wind gusts
The widest area of cloud
The heaviest total rainfall
questions.explanation: Cyclone categories from 1 to 5 are based on the strength of the strongest wind gusts, with Category 5 gusts above about 280 km/h. A large or slow cyclone can still bring huge rainfall and flooding even at a low category. That is why warnings describe rain and storm surge separately from the category.

questions.stem: Before cyclone season, a family in Townsville packs an emergency kit and plans an evacuation route. Which stage of hazard management is this?
options: Prevention
Preparedness
Recovery
Response
questions.explanation: Preparedness means getting ready before a hazard strikes so that people can act quickly and safely. Response is what happens during and straight after the event, such as evacuating, and recovery is rebuilding afterwards. Packing a kit cannot prevent a cyclone, so it is not prevention.

questions.stem: After Cyclone Tracy destroyed much of Darwin on Christmas Day 1974, which change had the most lasting effect on reducing future damage?
options: Moving the city to a new site far inland
Banning all housing within 50 km of the coast
Building a high sea wall around the whole of Darwin Harbour
Stronger building codes for houses in cyclone areas
questions.explanation: Darwin was rebuilt on the same site, but new houses had to meet much tougher building standards, such as roofs tied down to the frame, so homes could withstand cyclone winds. Building codes are a mitigation strategy because they reduce the damage when a cyclone does hit.

questions.stem: Why can a levee that protects a town from frequent small floods lead to more damage when a very large flood arrives?
options: Levees stop the Bureau of Meteorology from measuring river heights
Levees make the river shallower, so even small floods spill out
People build more behind it, and water that overtops it is trapped
Levees increase the amount of rain that falls over the whole catchment
questions.explanation: A levee gives a sense of safety, so more homes and businesses are built behind it, and when a flood is higher than the levee, water pours over and cannot drain away quickly. That is why planners combine levees with flood warnings, evacuation plans and limits on building in the lowest areas. Levees do not change how much rain falls.

questions.stem: What is the difference between urbanisation and urban growth?
options: Urbanisation is a rising share of people in cities; urban growth is a rising number
Urbanisation is a rising number of people in cities; urban growth is a rising share
Urbanisation happens in poorer countries; urban growth happens only in rich ones
Urbanisation means taller buildings; urban growth means cities spreading over more ground
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is about proportion: the percentage of a country's people living in urban areas goes up. Urban growth is about size: a city gains more people or covers more land. A city can grow while urbanisation stays the same, if the countryside is growing at the same rate.

questions.stem: What is chain migration?
options: Migrants moving in stages, from a village to a town and then on to a big city
Workers moving back and forth between home and a job each season
People forced to leave their country because of war or persecution
Migrants following family or friends who have already settled in a new place
questions.explanation: In chain migration, early migrants send back news, money or help, and relatives and neighbours from the same area follow them, which is why some suburbs have strong links to particular villages overseas. Moving in stages from village to town to city is step migration, a different pattern. Moving back and forth each season is circular migration.

questions.stem: Under international law, a refugee is a person who:
options: Has moved to another country to take up a better-paid job
Has been forced from their home but still lives inside their own country
Has stayed in a country after their visa has run out
Has fled their country because of a well-founded fear of persecution
questions.explanation: The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as someone outside their own country who cannot safely return because of a well-founded fear of persecution, for example because of their religion, race or political opinion. People forced from their homes who stay within their own country are called internally displaced people, not refugees. Moving for a better job is voluntary labour migration.

questions.stem: Workers from Vanuatu come to Australia each year to pick fruit for a season and then return home. What type of migration is this?
options: Chain migration
Circular migration
Permanent migration
Forced migration
questions.explanation: Circular migration is a repeated, temporary movement between home and a place of work, often following harvest seasons. Under Australia's Pacific labour schemes, workers earn money that they send home to support families and communities. It is not permanent migration because the workers return home rather than settling.

questions.stem: Why did mining booms in the Pilbara and the Bowen Basin bring large numbers of fly-in fly-out (FIFO) workers rather than new permanent towns?
options: Flying workers in was cheaper and more flexible than building whole new towns
Mining companies are banned by law from building towns near their mines
The mines only operate for a few weeks of each year, during the northern dry season
Workers must live in a capital city to keep their mining licence valid
questions.explanation: Building and servicing a remote town with houses, schools and hospitals is costly, and a mine may close when prices fall, so many companies chose to fly workers in from Perth, Brisbane and other cities for blocks of shifts. This shaped internal migration: workers kept their homes in the cities. Critics argue it weakens nearby regional towns that miss out on residents and spending.

questions.stem: How does China's hukou (household registration) system affect people who move from rural villages to cities?
options: It gives rural migrants first choice of public housing and of jobs in the big cities
It is a tax that rural families pay on land they leave behind
Their registration stays in their home area, limiting access to city services
It stops anyone from moving from the countryside into a large city
questions.explanation: Hukou ties each person to a registered home area, so migrants working in cities have often found it hard to get local schooling, health care or pensions there. It did not stop the huge movement to cities, which became one of the largest migrations in history. Reforms have eased the rules in many cities, but large gaps remain.

questions.stem: Why are many children in rural China described as 'left-behind children'?
options: They stayed in the village after their families emigrated overseas
They were sent to big cities to attend boarding schools for rural students
Their parents work in distant cities while they stay with grandparents
They left school early to work on family farms in the countryside
questions.explanation: Tens of millions of parents migrated to factory and construction jobs in cities, but city schooling and housing were hard to access, so children stayed behind in villages, usually with grandparents. The money sent home helps families, but researchers have found effects on children's wellbeing and schooling. This is one impact of urbanisation on the places migrants leave.

questions.stem: The Boston–Washington corridor in the USA, where large cities have merged into one long urban region, is an example of a:
options: Rural-urban fringe
Megalopolis
Primate city
Satellite town
questions.explanation: A megalopolis is a chain of large cities and their suburbs that have grown together along a transport corridor, here from Boston through New York and Philadelphia to Washington. A primate city is a single city far larger than any other in its country. The USA has several such corridors, which is one way its urban pattern differs from Australia's.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a decentralisation strategy?
options: Building many more apartments close to the centre of the capital city
Releasing new housing estates on the city's outer edge
Adding new freeway lanes into the central business district
Moving government offices from a capital city to regional centres
questions.explanation: Decentralisation tries to spread population and jobs away from the biggest cities, for example by moving government agencies to regional cities or building planned centres such as Canberra. Building apartments near the city centre is urban consolidation, which concentrates people further. New fringe estates are urban sprawl, which still adds to the big city.

questions.stem: Why is Australia's urban population concentrated in a few coastal capitals, while the USA has a more even spread of large cities?
options: Australia's population is larger than the USA's, so it is crowded into fewer cities
Australia's cities are younger, so inland cities have not yet had time to grow
Each colony grew around a port capital, and the dry interior supports few people
Australia's government has always banned the building of new inland cities
questions.explanation: Each Australian colony was run from one port city that handled its trade and government, and much of the inland is too dry for dense settlement, so about two-thirds of Australians live in the capital cities. The USA has a large, well-watered interior with navigable rivers, railways and resources that supported many big inland cities such as Chicago. Australia's population is far smaller than the USA's.

questions.stem: A Pacific nation trains nurses who then migrate to work in Australia and New Zealand. Which consequence for the home country is described as 'brain drain'?
options: Receiving money sent home by the nurses to support their families
Gaining new skills when the nurses return home after several years
Having fewer people overall, which reduces pressure on local housing and schools
Losing skilled workers it paid to train, which weakens its health services
questions.explanation: Brain drain is the loss of educated, skilled people to other countries, which can leave hospitals short-staffed and waste the money spent on training. Money sent home, called remittances, is a benefit of migration rather than brain drain. Returning migrants who bring back skills are the opposite effect, sometimes called brain gain.
